description: AI/ML and software-focused builder working across data science, cybersecurity, robotics, and space tech. Building TERRA - SNSX for NASA Space Apps, a planetary analogue platform combining NASA Earth, Moon, and Mars data, GIS, AI, and 3D visualisation. Seeking teammates in planetary science, GIS, ML, data, 3D, UI/UX, and research. Curiosity and ownership matter most.
summary:
SNSX SPACE is an open-source, end-to-end web platform for planetary analogue research. Given a 40 × 40 km reference window on the Moon (LRO LOLA) or Mars (MGS MOLA), it screens real Earth terrain from AWS Terrain Tiles, re-measures the strongest candidates from Copernicus DEM GLO-30 on the same 500 m grid, and ranks them using transparent geomorphology, morphometry, texture, and operational features. Similarity, confidence, and evidence are reported separately: every score is traceable to a source product, citation, resolution, valid-pixel fraction, and processing method, and missing data is never invented. The platform includes a Next.js/Three.js interface with real DEM terrain meshes, a FastAPI/PostGIS backend with a durable job queue, and PDF, CSV, GeoJSON, and JSON reports with reproducibility manifests. Independent Planetary Computer and Meteomatics cross-checks add context without changing scores.

It directly addresses the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge — identifying Earth locations that analog permanent Moon-base sites and Mars environments — by turning a visual, manual search into a reproducible, evidence-weighted workflow. This matters for mission planning, site selection, operations, and resource studies, where transparent uncertainty is as important as the ranking itself.
details:
SNSX SPACE is a working planetary-analogue platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 problem: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.

VISIT SNSX SPACE

A user selects a 40 × 40 km reference window on the Moon or Mars. The platform reads the real DEM — LRO LOLA at roughly 237 m/pixel for the Moon, MGS MOLA at 463 m for Mars — and resamples it to a common 500 m grid. It then screens real Earth terrain from AWS Terrain Tiles, re-measures the strongest candidates from Copernicus DEM GLO-30 on the identical 500 m geometry, and ranks them using four declared dimensions: geomorphology (35%), morphometry (30%), texture (20%), and operational proxies (15%).

Every result separates three things that are often conflated: similarity (how close the measured terrain is), confidence (how complete, valid, resolved, and method-consistent the evidence is), and evidence (the product, citation, resolution, valid-pixel fraction, and processing method behind each number). Missing dimensions are excluded and remaining weights renormalized; they are never imputed. Completed runs produce interactive rankings, real 3D elevation meshes built from the same DEM, and PDF, CSV, GeoJSON, and JSON reports with a reproducibility manifest.

Benefits

- Traceable and reproducible: every displayed value maps to a stored observation and source product.

- Evidence-first: low-quality evidence is shown as low confidence, not hidden behind a single score.

- No invented data: unavailable services return an explicit error or a recorded fallback, never synthetic terrain.

- Practical: runs on a standard laptop with no GPU and no paid API required for the core workflow.

- Operational: durable PostGIS-backed job queue, live progress, retries, cancellation, and auditable exports.

Intended Impact

The project turns a slow, visual, expert-driven search into a repeatable screening workflow for lunar and Martian analogue studies. It supports mission planning, site selection, operations and resource research, geology education, and public engagement — while stating clearly that similarity is a heuristic lead, not a probability, a geological interpretation, or a landing-safety recommendation.

Tools, languages, and software

- Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2, Alembic, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, pyproj, Shapely, ReportLab.

- Database and queue: PostgreSQL 16 with PostGIS 3.4; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED job queue; optional Redis profile.

- Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Three.js.

- Infrastructure: Docker and Docker Compose, uv, Node 22, GitHub Actions CI, optional Cloudflare Quick Tunnel for public hosting.

- Scientific data: USGS LRO LOLA and MGS MOLA, Copernicus DEM GLO-30, AWS Terrain Tiles, NASA GIBS/CMR, ESA WorldCover, Sentinel-2, Landsat, Microsoft Planetary Computer, OpenStreetMap Nominatim, optional NASA FIRMS and Meteomatics.

- Hardware: ordinary laptop or workstation; no specialized hardware, GPU, or paid service is required.

How the project is creative

The core idea is like-with-like measurement. Both reference and candidate are forced onto the same physical footprint and grid before any comparison, so resolution differences cannot masquerade as terrain differences. A cheap coarse screen narrows the planet; an expensive Copernicus refinement only visits the survivors. The platform then keeps similarity and confidence separate, exposes method disagreement, and cross-checks DEMs and land cover with independent Planetary Computer products without letting those context layers change the score. Real 3D terrain is generated from the same measured DEM rather than decorative imagery, and every run ships with the manifest needed to reproduce it.

Factors we considered

We designed around cross-body datum differences (absolute elevation is never compared), resolution mismatch, missing coverage, method disagreement, and the risk of overstating weak evidence. We also weighed performance on slow scientific archives (windowed reads and local caching instead of bulk downloads), credential safety (tokens never written to reports, logs, or manifests), public-deployment security (same-origin proxy, blocked admin and destructive routes, per-IP write limits), licensing and data attribution, and the need for the system to remain useful offline or without paid AI services.
